demand.question: Athena query quotas: default active DML and active DDL queries per Region (and that the count includes queued queries), DML query timeout default and its maximum (240 minutes per service-limits), DDL query timeout, query string length (262144 bytes, not adjustable). Which are adjustable?

Athena workgroup and partition limits: 1000 workgroups per Region per account; quotas shared across workgroups; 10 million partitions per Glue table but at most 1 million partitions read in a single scan; Athena needs a separate bucket for results. CTAS and INSERT INTO: at most 100 partitions written per query (ctas-insert-into).

Athena pricing dimensions: SQL queries charged per TB of data scanned with a 10 MB minimum per query (rounding unit); DDL and failed queries not charged; canceled queries charged for data scanned; capacity reservations charged per DPU (4 DPU minimum, 1-minute reservations since 2026-02-10); Athena for Apache Spark per DPU-hour; S3 and Glue Data Catalog charged separately.
demand.note: register-35 searched snap and full scopes again ('10 MB minimum', 'rounded up', DDL charges): the 10 MB minimum is stated only for federated queries (athena-price-federated-10-mb-minimum) and the per-query control floor (10 MB to 7 EB); no saved page says DDL queries are free. Writers must not state a 10 MB minimum for SQL queries on S3 or free DDL.

demand.question: How much do compression, partitioning and columnar formats save in Athena (FAQ 'Why do I get charged less when I use a columnar format?' and 'How do I lower my costs?'; pricing page example numbers such as savings of 30% to 90%)? Quote the AWS sentence with its condition.

AWS Glue quotas: databases per account, tables per database, partitions per table, table versions, jobs per account, concurrent job runs per job, maximum DPUs used by a role at one time, crawlers per account, concurrent crawlers; which are adjustable.

Glue DPU and worker types: what one DPU is (vCPU and memory), worker types G.1X, G.2X, G.4X, G.8X (and larger), R memory-optimized, G.025X for streaming, minimum workers; Python shell job capacity (0.0625 or 1 DPU); default job timeout.

Glue pricing dimensions: ETL jobs per DPU-hour billed per second with a minimum duration (by Glue version); Flex execution class price; crawlers per DPU-hour; Data Catalog storage and requests (free tier of the first million objects and requests); Data Quality; interactive sessions. Change: Glue 6.0 '30% price reduction' (2026-08-21, not examinable yet).

Lake Formation pricing and quotas: is there a charge for Lake Formation permissions (pricing page: what is charged, for example requests/data filtering/storage optimization, and that underlying services bill separately); Lake Formation quotas from the General Reference page (for example LF-Tags per account, values per tag, data filters).

EMR limits: instance types per instance fleet (console vs API/CLI), maximum instance groups and task instance groups per cluster, number of primary nodes in a high-availability cluster (3) and the release it needs; EMR API rate quotas; EMR Serverless default vCPU account quota.

EMR pricing dimensions: EMR on EC2 charged per second with a 1-minute minimum, on top of the EC2 (and EBS) price; On-Demand, Reserved, Savings Plans and Spot supported; EMR Serverless charged for vCPU, memory and storage used per second (aggregate, with a minimum); EMR on EKS. When does billing begin and end (FAQ)?

EMR HDFS replication factor defaults by core node count (dfs.replication) and what happens to HDFS data when a cluster terminates; how long logs are kept (FAQ 'How do I get logs for terminated clusters?').

OpenSearch Service quotas (card level): domains per Region per account, data nodes per domain, maximum EBS volume size per instance, UltraWarm nodes; OpenSearch Serverless collection limits (collections per collection group since 2026-08-10, not examinable yet).

OpenSearch Service pricing dimensions and snapshots: instance hours, EBS storage, UltraWarm and cold storage (managed storage), OpenSearch Serverless OCUs, automated snapshots (how often, how long kept, free of charge per FAQ), Multi-AZ with Standby (three AZs, availability), Extended Support charges for old engine versions.
SLA commitments for Athena, Glue, EMR and OpenSearch Service (monthly uptime percentages; OpenSearch Multi-AZ with Standby vs other deployments).

Amazon Quick (Quick Sight) limits: SPICE dataset size (rows and GB; 2 billion rows since 2025-07-02; expanded size since 2026-01-20), file upload sizes and data source quotas; SPICE refresh frequency limits (scheduled refresh, incremental refresh).

demand.question: Retired and closed answers: S3 Select closed to new customers (reuse s3-change-select-closed-to-new-customers-2024-07; FREQUENCY says Athena replaces it: confirm only with a page that says so); AWS Data Pipeline closed to new customers (maintenance list; does the page name Glue as the alternative?); Glue for Ray closed; Lake Formation Governed Tables shut down.

What Athena is: an interactive, serverless query service that analyzes data in S3 with standard SQL; no infrastructure to manage; pay per query; built on Trino/Presto (engine); results in seconds. When should Athena be used (when-should-i-use-ate)?

Athena tables and the Glue Data Catalog: Athena stores table definitions in the Glue Data Catalog; tables are metadata (schema-on-read) and the data stays in S3; dropping a table does not delete the S3 data; tables can be created with a crawler, a form or DDL; Athena integrates with other services (athena-aws-service-integrations).

Formats and performance in Athena: supported formats (CSV, TSV, JSON, Parquet, ORC, Avro, ...); why columnar Parquet/ORC plus compression plus partitioning reduce the data scanned and the cost; partition projection vs MSCK REPAIR TABLE / ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION; file size advice (avoid many small files).

Converting CSV or JSON to Parquet with Athena: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) with format and partitioning, INSERT INTO for later batches, UNLOAD to write query results in Parquet; CTAS limits (100 partitions; considerations).

Athena query results: written to an S3 query result location or to managed query results (no bucket to manage); result encryption options (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, CSE-KMS) and minimum encryption at the workgroup; query result reuse (cached results, max age).

Athena workgroups: separate users, teams and applications; enforce workgroup settings (result location, encryption) over client settings; per-query data usage limit (cancels the query) and per-workgroup data usage alarms; CloudWatch query metrics; tags for cost allocation. This is the exam answer for 'limit how much data a team can scan'.

Athena federated query: data source connectors run on Lambda and let SQL query DynamoDB, RDS, Redshift, CloudWatch Logs and other sources in place; joins across sources; managed connectors (2026-04-23). Athena queries of AWS service logs in S3 (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, ALB access logs).

Athena security: access needs IAM permissions for Athena and for the S3 data and result locations; cross-account access to another account's bucket (bucket policy); Lake Formation fine-grained permissions apply to Athena queries; querying SSE-S3/SSE-KMS/CSE-KMS encrypted data; interface VPC endpoint; S3 Glacier objects must be restored to be queried (querying-glacier); resilience across AZs.

Athena compute options: on-demand vs capacity reservations (dedicated DPUs for predictable concurrency); Athena for Apache Spark notebooks; Iceberg tables with ACID transactions (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, time travel); other limitations (other-notable-limitations).

What AWS Glue is: a serverless data integration service; its components (Data Catalog, crawlers and classifiers, ETL jobs: Spark, streaming, Python shell; triggers and workflows; Glue Studio visual ETL; Data Quality; data preparation recipes); engines (Spark; Ray closed to new customers).

The Glue Data Catalog: a persistent metadata store (databases, tables, partitions) per account per Region; Apache Hive metastore compatible; used by Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum and Lake Formation; ways to populate it (crawlers, DDL, API, other services); encryption of catalog metadata with KMS; resource policies and cross-account access; partition indexes; best practices.

Glue crawlers: what they do (connect to a data store, use classifiers to infer schema, create or update tables and partitions in the Data Catalog); supported data stores; schedules; incremental crawls with S3 event notifications; preventing schema changes.

Glue ETL for format conversion: Spark jobs read CSV/JSON and write Parquet (format options; Parquet writer); Relationalize flattens nested JSON; job bookmarks process only new data since the last run; visual ETL in Glue Studio; triggers (schedule, on-demand, conditional/job events) and workflows; EventBridge events.

Glue streaming ETL (sources Kinesis Data Streams, Kafka/MSK; micro-batches) and when to choose Glue vs Data Firehose, Glue vs EMR, Glue vs DMS, Glue vs Batch (FAQ comparison answers; behavior lens adds guide facts, FAQ lens the quick-fire answers).

Glue data protection features: sensitive data (PII) detection in ETL jobs with actions (redact, hash); Glue Data Quality (rules, recommendations, anomaly detection); Glue Studio no-code data preparation (DataBrew recipes; DataBrew migration page).

Glue security: jobs and crawlers assume an IAM role; security configurations encrypt S3 output, CloudWatch Logs and job bookmarks with KMS; connections to data stores in a VPC (ENIs in a subnet, security group self-reference, S3 gateway endpoint); interface VPC endpoints for the Glue API; Lake Formation access control models for Glue.

Glue zero-ETL integrations (sources such as DynamoDB and SaaS applications, targets such as Redshift and SageMaker lakehouse) and the Glue Schema Registry (reuse kinesis-data-streams-faq-glue-schema-registry-support); one fact each, recognise level.

What Lake Formation is: a service to centrally govern, secure and share data for analytics; it builds on the Glue Data Catalog; components and terminology (data lake administrator, data location, registered location, LF-Tags, data filters, resource links); integrated services (Athena, Redshift Spectrum, Glue, EMR, Quick).

Lake Formation permission model: Lake Formation permissions combined with IAM permissions; metadata permissions vs underlying data (storage) permissions; registering an S3 location with a role so Lake Formation vends temporary credentials (credential vending); default settings for new databases and tables (IAMAllowedPrincipals / 'Use only IAM access control') and the upgrade to the Lake Formation model; hybrid access mode; data location permissions; initial setup (data lake administrator).

Lake Formation fine-grained access: column-level, row-level and cell-level security with data filters (and their limitations); tag-based access control (LF-TBAC) to scale permissions; named resource method; which engines enforce it (athena-lf, emr-integ-lf, qs-integ-lf). This answers 'analysts must not see columns with personal data'.

Lake Formation sharing and audit: cross-account sharing (AWS RAM, to accounts, OUs, organizations or IAM principals), resource links, cross-data sharing; IAM Identity Center integration; encryption at rest of the catalog; CloudTrail logging of data access (monitoring-overview); blueprints and workflows to ingest data (built on Glue).

Building a data lake on S3 (whitepapers): S3 as the central storage platform; decouple storage from compute; ingestion methods; catalog and search; transform raw data into curated formats; in-place querying (Athena, Redshift Spectrum); securing (IAM, KMS, Lake Formation); monitoring and future-proofing; the serverless pipeline layers (ingestion, storage, catalog, processing, consumption, security and governance) and S3 zones (raw, cleaned, curated).

What Amazon EMR is: a managed cluster platform that runs big data frameworks (Apache Hadoop, Spark, Hive, Presto/Trino, HBase, Flink); deployment options EMR on EC2, EMR on EKS, EMR Serverless (and Outposts); when to choose EMR (existing Spark/Hadoop jobs, full control of the cluster and open-source configuration).

EMR node types and resilience: primary node (manages the cluster), core nodes (run tasks and store HDFS data), task nodes (run tasks, no HDFS, suit Spot); a cluster runs in one Availability Zone; multiple primary nodes for high availability; what happens when core nodes are lost; unhealthy node replacement.

EMR storage and cluster lifecycle: HDFS on instance store/EBS is ephemeral (lost at termination) vs EMRFS on S3 persistent; decouple storage and compute; transient (auto-terminating after steps) vs long-running clusters; auto-termination policy after idle time; termination protection; submitting steps.

EMR cost and scaling: purchasing options (On-Demand, Reserved, Spot) per node type; the guideline to run task nodes (not primary/core for long-running) on Spot; instance fleets (several instance types, allocation strategies, Spot with On-Demand fallback) vs uniform instance groups; managed scaling vs custom automatic scaling policies.

EMR Serverless and choosing compute for data processing: no clusters to configure; applications, workers, pre-initialized capacity; automatic scaling; Spark and Hive; compare Athena for Apache Spark vs EMR Serverless (FAQ), Glue vs EMR (FAQ), and the analytics-lens best practice for choosing compute (decouple storage from compute; serverless for unpredictable workloads).

EMR security: security configurations (at-rest encryption for EMRFS on S3 and local disks, in-transit TLS); IAM service role and EC2 instance profile (permissions of the cluster's applications); block public access (on by default; port 22 exception); managed security groups; private subnets; Lake Formation integration for fine-grained access; IAM access to EMR.

OpenSearch Service (service card): what it is (managed OpenSearch, formerly Elasticsearch; search, log analytics, observability, vector search); domains and OpenSearch Dashboards; ingestion (Data Firehose, OpenSearch Ingestion, Logstash, DynamoDB zero-ETL: reuse dynamodb facts); OpenSearch Serverless collections vs managed domains; storage tiers hot/UltraWarm/cold (S3-backed); dedicated master nodes; Multi-AZ with Standby; VPC access vs public endpoint; fine-grained access control, Cognito for Dashboards, encryption at rest and node-to-node; direct query of S3 data.

Amazon Quick (service card): what Amazon Quick is and that Quick Sight is its BI part (formerly Amazon QuickSight); dashboards and analyses; SPICE in-memory engine vs direct query; data sources (Athena, Redshift, RDS/Aurora, S3, OpenSearch, SaaS); row-level security (and column-level security if stated); embedding dashboards for registered and anonymous users; VPC connections to private data sources; Lake Formation and Athena integration; ML insights (anomaly detection) and generative BI; identity options (IAM Identity Center).

AWS Data Exchange (service card): find, subscribe to and use third-party data in the cloud; data products contain data sets of files (exported to S3), APIs, Redshift datashares, S3 data access and Lake Formation data (preview); revisions and auto-export jobs to S3; providers and subscribers; data grants; difference from the Registry of Open Data on AWS.

The analytics decision guide and overview: which service AWS names for each analytics need (interactive SQL on S3, big data processing, data warehouse, search and log analytics, BI dashboards, data catalog and ETL, governance, data sharing); the AWS overview sentences for Athena, EMR, Glue, Lake Formation, OpenSearch, Quick and Data Exchange; reuse kinesis-data-streams-decision-streaming-category for streaming.
demand.note: decision guide says Glue connects to more than 100 data sources; the stored Glue FAQ fact says more than 70. The 100 figure was not added as a fact; the writer should use the FAQ/guide fact as verified and avoid the number.

demand.question: The comparison the exam hinges on (FREQUENCY section 3): Athena (ad-hoc SQL on S3, serverless) vs Redshift (data warehouse for complex, frequent BI queries; Redshift Spectrum queries S3) vs EMR (Spark/Hadoop clusters you control) vs Glue (serverless ETL and catalog). Use the Athena FAQ comparison answers, the big-data whitepaper sections ('ideal usage patterns', 'anti-patterns') and the Redshift Spectrum page.

All the ways to turn CSV or JSON into Parquet and why: Glue ETL job (d036), Athena CTAS (d027), Data Firehose record format conversion (reuse data-firehose-format-conversion-json-to-parquet-orc and data-firehose-format-conversion-needs-glue-schema), EMR Spark; analytics-lens advice on choosing a format and partitioning by access pattern; Parquet is columnar and compressed.

Data access and governance across the stack: least-privilege data access with IAM plus bucket policies plus Lake Formation; KMS encryption of data and catalog; audit with CloudTrail; Well-Architected Analytics Lens BP 4.3 (data access authorization models) and the lens introduction; the serverless pipeline's security and governance layer.

Visualization strategy: Quick dashboards on Athena or Redshift; SPICE import vs direct query trade-off (speed vs freshness); embedding for customers; OpenSearch Dashboards for log and search analytics; Well-Architected data-visualization scenario (characteristics, reference architecture); serverless pipeline consumption layer.

Callvale decision (STARTUP.md chapter 35; story values are not facts): option 1 'a larger replica for analysts' (reuse aurora-replicas-offload-reads, aurora-custom-endpoint-use-different-instance-classes-reporting, rds-read-replica-all-databases: a replica copies all data, including personal-data columns); option 2 'a data warehouse for all data' (Redshift, chapter 30: reuse or point to d056); option 3 chosen: S3 data lake with Glue crawlers and jobs (JSON to Parquet), Athena (SQL with no infrastructure, pay per query), Lake Formation column-level permissions (hide personal-data columns), OpenSearch Service for transcript full-text search, Quick for dashboards. Accepts: data must be converted (Glue job) and results are only as fresh as the last load (scheduled trigger, job bookmarks). Ana's question: why analysts should not query production (replica offload vs isolation). List the fact ids each reason cites.
